Local communities connected to the forest and river economy, including fishermen and market workers in cities like Belém, are also affected by these ongoing environmental and economic challenges.

1220944_1220944.caption: A miner leaving Kellingley colliery the UK s last deep coal mine for the final time
1220944_1220944.article_context: Kellingley colliery, the UK's last deep coal mine, is closing after 50 years, marking the end of an industry that once employed over a million people nationwide. The closure comes amid shifts towards renewable energy, increased carbon taxes, and reliance on imported coal, leaving 451 workers facing an uncertain future and many receiving only minimal redundancy pay. Miners express frustration and sadness over the loss of their jobs, camaraderie, and financial security, and criticize political decisions dating back to the Thatcher era that contributed to the decline of coal mining. The final ton of coal extracted will be preserved as a historical artifact, symbolizing the end of an era for British coal mining.

457207_457207.caption: Jim Ratcliffe In the US they have drilled one million wells and not had an environmental incident for six years
457207_457207.article_context: Jim Ratcliffe, billionaire founder of chemicals giant Ineos, argues that the UK's energy policy is flawed due to its heavy reliance on traditional energy sources and inconsistent wind generation. Ratcliffe advocates for fracking, suggesting it could ease supply concerns, lower energy costs, and revitalize northern industrial regions. Ineos has recently acquired multiple UK fracking licenses and invested in shipping ethane gas from the US to Europe, citing US shale success and safe practices. The article also notes UK government interest in fracking, and Ratcliffe’s criticism of Britain’s decline in manufacturing and skilled labor, calling for more emphasis on industrial vitality and competitive energy costs.

673495_673495.caption: The Putaya River in Peru s Ucayali department where illegal logging persists
673495_673495.article_context: Four indigenous Ashéninka leaders from the Peruvian Amazon, including Jorge Rios Perez, were murdered in September after opposing illegal logging in their territory, believed to be associated with drug-traffickers. Despite arrests of two suspects, the widows and families of the victims fear for their safety and have fled their village due to ongoing threats and continued logging activities. The community criticizes the government and police for inadequate protection and ineffective law enforcement, while legal title to their land and demands for justice and proper protection remain unresolved. The case highlights broader struggles faced by indigenous communities against illegal logging in Peru and the lack of adequate institutional support.

1035061_1035061.caption: RatcliffeonSoar power station in Nottinghamshire will be targeted by protesters on October 17
1035061_1035061.article_context: Ahead of the planned Great Climate Swoop protest at Ratcliffe-on-Soar coal power station, police arrested an environmental activist on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, following earlier charges against 25 activists for conspiracy to commit aggravated trespass. This approach marks a shift toward preventative policing and tougher legal measures, raising concerns among environmentalists about increased deterrence and restrictions on activist communications and activities.

97821_97821.caption: People demonstrate against Iceland s Prime Minister Sigmundur Gunnlaugsson in Reykjavik on April 4 REUTERSStigtryggur Johannsson
97821_97821.article_context: Iceland's Prime Minister, Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson, resigned after revelations that his wife held millions in investments in the country’s largest banks, creating potential conflicts of interest while he was in office. The leaks, part of the ‘Panama Papers’, showed Gunnlaugsson and his wife used offshore companies to shelter their investments during the 2008 financial crisis, which devastated ordinary Icelanders and fueled public anger. Massive protests erupted in Reykjavík, highlighting lingering resentment over the crisis and suspicions that Gunnlaugsson did not share the same stakes as other citizens. Although there is no clear evidence of illegal activity, the controversy over undisclosed personal financial ties and possible benefit from political decisions led to his downfall.

1611506_1611506.caption: Staff have been locked out of the Caterham Sports Limited site in Leafield
1611506_1611506.article_context: Staff at the Caterham F1 team's Oxfordshire site have been locked out after administrators took control of the building due to financial troubles. The administrator, Finbarr O'Connell, cited an inadequate offer from the team operator, 1MRT, for continued use of the site. Around 200 jobs are at risk and up to £20m is owed to suppliers, raising uncertainty about the team's future and its ability to compete in upcoming Formula 1 races. The situation follows recent ownership changes and confusion over company responsibilities.

1642244_1642244.caption: The minimum wage for Isle of Man workers aged 21 or over will be 15p higher than the UK
1642244_1642244.article_context: The Isle of Man government has announced that the minimum wage for workers aged 21 or over will rise by 25p to £6.65 per hour from 1 October, following approval by Tynwald. This increase places the Isle of Man's rate above that of the UK, which will be £6.50, and on par with Guernsey, which will also raise its minimum wage to £6.65. Workers aged 18-20 on the island will continue to receive £6.40, while rates for those aged 16 and 17 remain unchanged.

1601295_1601295.caption: More than 800 jobs will be lost at BAE s Govan and Scotstoun shipyards
1601295_1601295.article_context: Following BAE Systems' announcement that it will cut 1,775 jobs at its UK shipyards, including more than 800 positions in Glasgow, the Scottish government has pledged support to help affected workers find new employment or retrain. Deputy First Minister Nicola Sturgeon stated that details of the redundancies will be clarified next week, after which targeted assistance will be provided. The government sees opportunities for displaced workers in other engineering sectors and is coordinating with unions and BAE management to ease the transition. Meanwhile, BAE and the Ministry of Defence will build three new offshore patrol vessels at Govan and Scotstoun to help sustain shipbuilding activities until work on the Type 26 combat ships begins after 2014.

162886_162886.caption: We came really close here we got to the precipice of putting uncomfortable restrictions on Uber said Illinois state Rep Michael Zalewski
162886_162886.article_context: Uber responded to regulatory challenges in Virginia by mobilizing its customer base to pressure officials and deploying a large network of lobbyists, successfully overturning a cease-and-desist order and influencing the creation of new temporary operating permits. This approach—entering markets without regulatory approval, then leveraging public support and political influence—has enabled Uber to reshape transportation laws across numerous states, winning legislative victories and expanding its operations rapidly. The company’s tactics, including mass email campaigns, app alerts, and high-powered lobbying led by figures like former Obama adviser David Plouffe, have disrupted traditional political alliances and received both support and criticism. Although Uber has faced legal battles, privacy concerns, and occasional setbacks, its aggressive strategy has made it a significant force in the tech and transportation industries, with regulators now focused on how best to govern ride-sharing services rather than whether they should be allowed to operate.

1535733_1535733.caption: Europe needs to adopt clearer policies on energy to encourage investors says a House of Lords report
1535733_1535733.article_context: A House of Lords inquiry has found that the EU needs €1 trillion in energy investment by the end of the decade to prevent an energy crisis. The report blames unclear EU energy policies for deterring investors despite available funds. It urges revision of the EU's Emissions Trading System, including setting a minimum carbon price, and recommends establishing a 2030 renewable energy target. The report also calls for better electricity inter-connections between member states and the development of regulations for shale gas exploitation.

343673_343673.caption: Diane Hendricks Wisconsin s richest woman did not pay personal state income taxes for four of five years Hendricks is vice chair of the Trump Victory fundraising committee
343673_343673.article_context: Diane Hendricks, Wisconsin’s wealthiest woman and vice chair of the Trump Victory fundraising committee, paid no state income taxes from 2012 to 2014, according to newly obtained records. Despite her net worth of nearly $5 billion and ownership of ABC Supply Co., Hendricks had a string of zero-tax years, except for notable payments in 2011 and 2015. Her tax history has drawn attention due to her political connections, including major donations to Republican campaigns, and parallels to controversies around Donald Trump’s taxes. Hendricks’ representatives and accountants cited common business fluctuations and legal deductions as possible reasons for her varying tax liabilities.

236864_236864.caption: CNN s Candy Crowley moderates the second of three presidential debates between President Obama and Republican Presidential nominee Mitt Romney
236864_236864.article_context: In their second debate, President Obama and Mitt Romney addressed key issues raised by undecided voters, including jobs, energy, education, deficit, China, immigration, gas prices, and the Benghazi attack. Fact checks revealed some of Romney's claims, such as his pledge to create 12 million jobs, were in line with economic forecasts rather than his specific plans. Both candidates clarified positions on energy production, education funding, and immigration laws, with nuanced differences. Obama was criticized for not halving the deficit, though it was not doubled as Romney claimed. Romney's business ties to China and Bain Capital were scrutinized, as were his past '47%' comments, which he later called a mistake. The fact checking showed that while both candidates made declarative statements, many were oversimplified or misleading, with actual outcomes and policy details more complex than presented in the debate.

1543159_1543159.caption: Two exRabobank traders are charged by the US Justice Department with manipulating the Libor rate bringing the total number of traders charged to six
1543159_1543159.article_context: Two former Rabobank traders, Anthony Allen and Anthony Conti, have been charged by the US Department of Justice for conspiring to manipulate the Libor benchmark interest rate for the bank’s financial benefit. These charges bring the total number of indicted Rabobank employees to six, as similar allegations were previously made against other former traders. The indictment follows Rabobank’s payment of €774 million in fines to US, British, and Dutch regulators over Libor manipulation.

236213_236213.caption: This June 2013 photo provided by The Guardian newspaper shows National Security Agency leaker Edward Snowden in Hong Kong
236213_236213.article_context: Federal authorities have accused US Investigations Services (USIS), a major government contractor, of fraudulently submitting 665,000 incomplete background checks between 2008 and 2012 in exchange for increased bonus payments. Roughly 40% of the company's investigations were allegedly released without proper review through a practice called 'dumping,' prioritized to boost revenue and meet internal quotas. The legal case is not linked to the company's work involving Edward Snowden or Aaron Alexis. USIS claims the issue involved only a few individuals and asserts that it has since strengthened its oversight and quality control.

169154_169154.caption: Jordanian protesters chant slogans during a demonstration against a government agreement to import natural gas from Israel in Amman Jordan Sept 30 2016
169154_169154.article_context: Thousands of Jordanians protested in Amman against a $10 billion natural gas deal recently signed with Israeli investors, accusing the government of supporting the occupation of Palestinian land and undermining Jordan’s advocacy for Palestinian rights. The agreement, which will provide 40% of Jordan’s energy needs from the Israeli Leviathan gas field, is intended to reduce budget deficits and stabilize energy costs, but faces strong opposition over fears that it will financially aid Israel and compromise Jordan’s political stance. Despite widespread public and parliamentary opposition, the government pushed forward with the deal, leading to concerns about public trust and representation.

94781_94781.caption: Puerto Rico urges US bankruptcy deal
94781_94781.article_context: Puerto Rico’s governor Alejandro Garcia Padilla announced the island cannot pay back its over $70 billion debt, calling for debt payments to be postponed for several years in order to revive economic growth. This declaration marks an unprecedented financial crisis that could destabilize the U.S. municipal bond market, as many Americans hold Puerto Rican bonds in their mutual funds. Puerto Rico is unable to file for bankruptcy protection, leaving creditors and the government facing an uncertain and potentially prolonged process to resolve its financial obligations. The governor emphasized the need for shared sacrifices and cooperation from creditors, citing the worsening economy and unsustainable debt as driving factors behind the crisis.

1665912_1665912.caption: BlaBlaCar s founder and chief executive Frederic Mazella says becoming a unicorn firm is the beginning
1665912_1665912.article_context: BlaBlaCar, founded by Frederic Mazella in 2006 as a long-distance ride-sharing platform, was created to address the issue of underutilized car seats for long journeys. After gaining popularity and investment, BlaBlaCar was valued at $1.6 billion, earning it the 'unicorn' status among privately-owned tech start-ups. The article discusses the significance and challenges of being labeled a unicorn, noting that such high valuations by private investors can be controversial and do not always reflect true market value. Other entrepreneurs, like Prezi's Peter Arvai and Virgin's Richard Branson, stress that building a successful company should focus on customers and innovation rather than on achieving high valuations.

1619396_1619396.caption: Troubled online gamemaker Zynga reports a loss of 61m as founder Mark Pincus steps down as chief product officer
1619396_1619396.article_context: Zynga, the online game-maker, reported a first-quarter loss of $61 million, widening from the previous quarter, and announced that founder Mark Pincus will end his executive roles, remaining only as board chairman. Despite continued losses and ongoing restructuring, including staff cuts and management changes, Zynga's shares rose as results were better than some investors expected. The company foresees further losses in the next quarter and does not expect to return to profitability soon.

1674289_1674289.caption: The city of Providence and other US investors are suing Petrobras over losses due to a corruption scandal
1674289_1674289.article_context: The US city of Providence, Rhode Island is suing Brazil’s state-run oil company Petrobras and some of its senior executives over investor losses from a corruption scandal, alleging false statements that inflated company value. The scandal has led to the indictment of 39 people in Brazil for corruption, money laundering, and racketeering involving overpriced contracts and political kickbacks. The case has shaken President Dilma Rousseff’s government, with courts blocking assets and investigating billions in suspicious transactions linked to Petrobras.

1577998_1577998.caption: Better productivity in the UK helped Ellesmere Port win the Astra over GM s other European plants
1577998_1577998.article_context: Vauxhall’s Ellesmere Port plant has secured a landmark deal to produce the new generation of Astra cars, with General Motors committing £125 million in investment and promising at least 160,000 cars annually. The agreement will create around 700 direct jobs and thousands more in the UK supply chain, backed by a £1 billion spend on UK components. Workers at the plant overwhelmingly voted for a flexible new labor agreement to support round-the-clock production, helping to secure its future amid GM’s broader European restructuring that may see other plants close. This development signals renewed confidence in UK manufacturing, with support from unions and the government, and reflects the country’s rising car production and competitiveness within the automotive sector.

1665367_1665367.caption: AirFrance pilots staged a twoweek strike in September over Air France s plans to expand its lowcost carrier
1665367_1665367.article_context: Air France-KLM reported that last month's pilots' strike led to a €416 million loss in revenue and caused its third-quarter operating profit to drop by more than half compared to last year. The airline expects the combined impact of the strike and weak market demand in the fourth quarter to reduce €500 million from its 2014 earnings target. In response, Air France-KLM plans to adjust investments, cut costs, and is considering selling assets such as its stake in Amadeus. The strike was triggered by plans to expand the budget carrier Transavia, which aims to compete with low-cost airlines, but has faced opposition from pilots due to pay disparities. The company denied rumors of major job cuts and is evaluating fleet options to further manage costs amid ongoing market challenges.

1456265_1456265.caption: The US Justice Department warned Bitcoin could be exploited by malicious actors
1456265_1456265.article_context: Bitcoin's value surpassed $1,000 for the first time, driven by growing legitimacy after a US Senate hearing recognized virtual currencies as valid financial services. Despite its connection to anonymous transactions and illegal activities like those on Silk Road, the crackdown on such sites did not dampen Bitcoin's value, which continued to rise amid regulatory optimism. The currency's rapid growth and volatility have sparked debate about its true nature, with some arguing it should be considered more like a commodity than traditional money. Increased global interest, especially in China, and new developments like Bitcoin ATMs indicate a growing acceptance of Bitcoin beyond its early niche users.

1506684_1506684.caption: Investigators looked at whether the Fukushima nuclear power station disaster affected Toshiba
1506684_1506684.article_context: Toshiba's chief executive Hisao Tanaka, along with several other senior executives, resigned after an independent investigation found the company had overstated its operating profits by 151.8 billion yen over six years. The accounting scandal, one of the worst in Toshiba’s history, involved widespread management pressure and inappropriate accounting practices dating back to the 2008 financial crash. The company will have to restate its earnings and faces potential fines and legal action, highlighting broader concerns about corporate governance in Japan. While the leadership shake-up aims to restructure Toshiba, analysts say the firm also faces ongoing challenges in competitiveness against global rivals and uncertainty about its future direction.

1537922_1537922.caption: US and UK regulators are continuing to investigate the raterigging scandal
1537922_1537922.article_context: UK broker ICAP was fined $87 million for its role in the Libor interest rate rigging scandal, and three of its former traders were charged with wire fraud in New York related to manipulating globally-used interest rate benchmarks. Regulators have been investigating Libor rate manipulation since 2012, implicating several major banks and resulting in hefty fines and criminal charges. The misconduct involved email exchanges that detailed attempts to fix Libor rates for personal gain, highlighting a culture of disregard for market integrity. In response, industry bodies have since revised procedures for setting the rates to prevent future manipulation.

1469865_1469865.caption: An investment from US firm Cargill will help boost Ukraine s grain exports
1469865_1469865.article_context: US agricultural firm Cargill has announced a $100 million investment to build a grain export terminal at a Ukrainian Black Sea port through a partnership with M.V. Cargo. This project aims to increase Ukraine's grain export capacity by five million tons annually, signaling renewed foreign investment despite the country's political instability and conflict with pro-Russian separatists. The terminal is expected to be completed by spring 2018 and supports Ukraine's ambition to become a leading agricultural exporter.

1550641_1550641.caption: Mr Modi wants India to be the human resources capital of the world
1550641_1550641.article_context: The Indian government has launched the Skills India initiative, aiming to provide vocational and technical training to over 400 million young people to improve their employability and address industry concerns about a lack of skilled workers. Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted the goal of making India the world's human resource capital, but critics point out that job creation remains a major challenge, with 12 million new jobs needed annually to maintain current unemployment levels. While only 2.3% of India’s workforce has formal skills training, far less than in other countries, both government and private sector programs are working to bridge the gap. However, the broader issue of job availability for the newly skilled workforce has yet to be fully addressed.

77731_77731.caption: Dozens of Museum Square apartments residents and their supporters rally Wednesday against eviction one day before the Chinatown building s Section 8 subsidy was to expire
77731_77731.article_context: Tenants of Museum Square apartments in Washington, D.C.'s Chinatown, many of whom are elderly Chinese immigrants, have rallied to protest their landlord's move to end their federal housing subsidy, which would raise rents to market rates. The property owner, Bush Companies, did not renew the Section 8 contract, but tenants have received vouchers under a new program that may allow them to remain if accepted. Disputes over rent payments and the building's fate continue, with legal action by residents challenging the owner's inflated sale price under the city's Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act. The struggle highlights broader concerns about the erosion of Chinatown's cultural community and the district's affordable housing crisis.

1518602_1518602.caption: Was that real or a spoof Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during the Flash Crash of 2010
1518602_1518602.article_context: U.S. prosecutors have begun charging traders with 'spoofing,' a form of market manipulation where traders place and then cancel large orders to influence prices. Notable cases include Navinder Singh Sarao, arrested in the UK and accused of contributing to the 2010 Flash Crash, and Michael Coscia, indicted in the US and fined $3 million for similar activities. These prosecutions follow the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, which explicitly banned spoofing, but the complexity of high frequency trading has made such cases difficult to investigate and prosecute. While some traders have faced civil penalties in the past, authorities are now pursuing more criminal cases to deter market manipulation.

275291_275291.caption: PRISM collects and analyzes communications stored by Internet companies It is overseen by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court
275291_275291.article_context: The Guardian reported that the NSA reimbursed major technology companies millions of dollars for costs related to the PRISM surveillance program after a 2011 secret court ruling found the agency had violated the Fourth Amendment by failing to separate domestic from overseas communications. Documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed these financial arrangements, marking the first clear evidence of a monetary relationship between the NSA and tech companies such as Google, Yahoo, Microsoft, and Facebook. While some companies acknowledged compliance with legal requests, most denied receiving government payments. The report follows revelations that the NSA has breached privacy rules thousands of times since 2008.

277975_277975.caption: In one of the largest acquisition deals ever Vodafone said Monday it sold its 45 stake in Verizon Wireless to Verizon Communications
277975_277975.article_context: Verizon Communications has agreed to buy the 45% stake in Verizon Wireless owned by U.K.-based Vodafone for $130 billion, in one of the largest acquisition deals in history. This move will give Verizon full ownership and control of its wireless unit, allowing it greater flexibility in managing growth in the expanding mobile data market. The deal, expected to close in early 2014, involves cash, Verizon shares, loan notes, and the transfer of Verizon’s interest in Vodafone Italy. Vodafone, facing declining revenues, will use the proceeds to invest in its European and emerging markets operations. The acquisition marks a significant shift in both companies' strategies and reflects the increasing importance of wireless services in telecommunications.

1499987_1499987.caption: Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras and EC President JeanClaude Juncker have been in weekend talks
1499987_1499987.article_context: With Greece facing a critical debt crisis and the threat of defaulting on a €1.6bn IMF repayment, emergency talks between Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras and eurozone leaders are underway to seek a resolution. The head of the National Bank of Greece emphasized the urgency of reaching an agreement, warning that failure could have severe consequences for the eurozone. Greece has proposed a deal aiming for a lasting solution, while its creditors demand economic reforms in areas such as pensions and VAT before releasing bailout funds. Disputes remain over pension cuts, tax policy, and credible reforms, with the outcome of Monday’s summit expected to determine whether Greece remains in the single currency or risks a financial crisis.

376195_376195.caption: President Obama greets members of Congress before his final State of the Union address on Jan 12 2016
376195_376195.article_context: In his final State of the Union Address, President Obama made several claims about his administration's achievements that were challenged for accuracy. He overstated job growth by focusing on private sector gains since 2010, omitting early job losses, and exaggerated manufacturing job recovery by selectively referencing data from the lowest point of his presidency. Obama also claimed to have significantly reduced the deficit, but this comparison started from a peak that included new spending initiated under his own administration. His assertion that the Affordable Care Act was primarily responsible for slowing health care spending was questioned, as economists credit broader economic factors and noted recent upticks in costs. Obama further stated the U.S. cut more carbon emissions than any other country, which is only true in absolute terms, not percentage reductions. Lastly, he referenced U.S. military spending as surpassing the next eight nations combined, which is accurate in dollar terms, but not when measured as a percentage of GDP. Overall, the address was marked by selective use of statistics and context omissions.

185779_185779.caption: US Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton talks to journalists during the third meeting of Contact Group on Libya on Thursday in Abu Dhabi United Arab Emirates
185779_185779.article_context: Speculation arose after a Reuters report claimed that Secretary of State Hillary Clinton was considering becoming the next World Bank president. The report triggered widespread media attention despite immediate and strong denials from Clinton's aides and the White House, insisting she had no interest in the post and had not discussed it with anyone. World Bank officials also noted uncertainty about a vacancy. Clinton herself did not comment directly, while her team worked to counter the persistent rumors.

1511254_1511254.caption: Dick Costolo chief executive of Twitter admits it has work to do
1511254_1511254.article_context: Twitter released data revealing significant gender and ethnic imbalances in its workforce, with only 30% female staff and under-representation of black and Hispanic employees compared to U.S. population figures. This disclosure follows similar admissions by Facebook, Google, and Yahoo, highlighting a broader diversity issue across the tech industry. Experts have called for urgent action to address these disparities, especially given greater gender gaps in leadership roles. Twitter acknowledged the challenges and stated its commitment to improving diversity.

1467008_1467008.caption: Mr Hannigan warned that Islamic State jihadists were using the net to intimidate people and radicalise new recruits
1467008_1467008.article_context: Robert Hannigan, the new director of British spy agency GCHQ, published an article stating that major tech companies have become favored platforms for terrorists and urged them to assist intelligence investigations. His comments sparked broad debate, with some supporting a public discussion about privacy, while critics suspect it is a prelude to expanding government surveillance powers. Media outlets, privacy advocates, and users online voiced concerns about eroding privacy rights, questioned GCHQ’s mass data collection practices, and called for judicial oversight. The controversy highlights a growing distrust between technology firms and government agencies, and emphasizes the need for an open, balanced debate on privacy versus security.

1619850_1619850.caption: It has been warned that the closure of Longannet power station could make Scotland dependent on power from south of the border
1619850_1619850.article_context: Scottish MSPs are investigating the security of the country's energy supply amid concerns over the closure of major thermal power plants like Longannet. With renewable energy not yet able to fully meet demand, Scotland risks electricity shortages and will increasingly depend on importing power from England until new infrastructure, such as sub-sea interconnectors, are completed. Energy companies warn that emergency plans need to be revised, back-up capacity must be improved, and the market requires more stable pricing and better incentives, especially for renewable energy and storage solutions. The situation highlights ongoing challenges with grid access charges, regional disparities, and the need for long-term policy stability as Scotland moves toward a low-carbon future.

1641645_1641645.caption: Mr Al Tikriti says his children are confused by HSBC s decision
1641645_1641645.article_context: HSBC has notified several UK-based Muslim organizations, including Finsbury Park Mosque, the Cordoba Foundation think tank, and Ummah Welfare Trust, that their accounts will be closed due to the bank's review of its risk policies. HSBC claims the closures are not related to race or religion, but affected groups and individuals have expressed concern over a perceived lack of transparency and potential discrimination, especially given their charitable activities and links to issues such as Palestine. The bank's actions are part of a global strategy following a $1.9 billion fine in 2012 for poor money-laundering controls, prompting wider scrutiny of account holders. Community leaders and local MPs have criticized the move, warning it could damage charitable operations and erode public trust.

1648194_1648194.caption: Mr Mundell said the figures were a reminder of the challenges facing Scotland s economy in particular in the oil and gas sector
1648194_1648194.article_context: Unemployment in Scotland increased by 16,000 between November and January, bringing the total to 171,000 and raising the unemployment rate to 6.1%, higher than the UK average. Despite this, Scottish employment rose by 17,000, with rates outperforming the UK average. Youth employment also reached its highest level since 2009. Officials highlighted ongoing challenges in the Scottish labour market, particularly due to the impact of low oil prices and global economic factors, and called for continued cooperation between Scottish and UK governments to support the economy, especially the oil and gas sector.

1580056_1580056.caption: US regulators announce that carmakers Hyundai and Kia have agreed to a record 100m settlement for overstating the fuel economy of their cars in violation of the Clean Air Act
1580056_1580056.article_context: US regulators announced that Hyundai and Kia have agreed to a record $350 million settlement for overstating the fuel economy of 1.2 million vehicles, including popular models such as Hyundai Accent, Elantra, Veloster, Santa Fe, and Kia Rio and Soul. The carmakers admitted exaggerating fuel efficiency and underreporting emissions, resulting in a $100 million penalty—the largest ever for Clean Air Act violations—along with the forfeiture of emissions credits and investment in compliance measures. The announcement led to a nearly 6% drop in both companies’ share prices.

43968_43968.caption: A woman shouts slogans and bangs on a pan last month during an antigovernment protest demanding the impeachment of Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff
43968_43968.article_context: Brazil’s economy has entered a severe recession, with shrinking growth, high inflation, rising unemployment, and a dramatic currency devaluation. The crisis has been worsened by a multibillion-dollar corruption scandal at state oil company Petrobras, leading to political instability and a major downgrade of Brazil’s credit rating to junk status by Standard & Poor’s. President Dilma Rousseff faces eroding popularity, coalition infighting, and potential impeachment, as her government struggles to introduce budgetary reforms amid divided opinions on austerity versus social spending. The turmoil has led to business closures, diminished investor confidence, and fears that further credit downgrades could deepen the recession.

328133_328133.caption: The convention at which Donald Trump will become the Republican presidential nominee opens Monday
328133_328133.article_context: Just days before the Republican National Convention begins in Cleveland, organizers are still $6 million short of their $64 million fundraising goal, facing challenges due to activist-led boycotts, withdrawn corporate sponsorships, and skepticism surrounding Donald Trump as the nominee. Despite these hurdles, the Cleveland committee claims they have managed expenses well and expect to fulfill all financial obligations. In contrast, the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia is nearly fully funded, aided by state financial support and intensive fundraising efforts. Both committees will only have to disclose their fundraising details 60 days after their respective conventions conclude.

1565205_1565205.caption: Only Centrica and Scottish and Southern Electricity remain in British ownership
1565205_1565205.article_context: The British confectionery giant Cadbury was acquired by US-based Kraft Foods in a controversial takeover in 2010, marking a shift away from its British roots as much of its operations and ownership were already international. The acquisition raised concerns about the impact of foreign ownership, including job losses—such as Kraft closing Cadbury’s Somerdale factory—and changes in tax jurisdictions, with Cadbury’s taxes now paid in Switzerland. The article highlights broader trends of traditionally British companies like Dyson, Clarks, and Boots moving production or ownership abroad, and notes that major UK infrastructure—such as ports, airports, and energy suppliers—is now predominantly foreign-owned. These developments raise questions about national identity, economic security, tax implications, and the global nature of modern business.

1484236_1484236.caption: Faroe said its drill test at the Pil exploration well showed a stable flow of oil
1484236_1484236.article_context: Faroe Petroleum’s share price rose over 10% after the company announced successful well results in the Norwegian Sea, including a gas and condensate discovery at Solberg and a successful oil flow test at Pil. Faroe holds significant stakes in both wells and estimates the Solberg discovery could yield up to 25 million barrels of oil equivalent. The finds are expected to enhance the commercial potential of adjacent fields, supporting Faroe’s strategy of investing in high-impact exploration prospects.

1534278_1534278.caption: NYSE Euronext profits were hit by failure of merger with Deutsche Boerse
1534278_1534278.article_context: NYSE Euronext reported a 19% decline in fourth quarter profits, largely due to the failed merger with Deutsche Boerse after European regulators blocked the deal over competition concerns. The company incurred $46 million in costs related to the collapsed merger and is now developing an alternative strategy, to be announced in April. In response, NYSE Euronext has launched a $550 million share buyback program and plans to expand its derivatives trading business. There are also rumors of a potential bid for LCH Clearnet, which is currently in talks with the London Stock Exchange.

174477_174477.caption: The 2016 Lexus RX 350 and other models dating back to 2014 lost functionality in their GPS climate control and radio systems because of a software glitch earlier this week
174477_174477.article_context: Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus faced a widespread software glitch that disabled GPS, climate control, and infotainment systems—including hands-free phone functions—in certain 2014-2016 Lexus vehicles and the 2016 Toyota Land Cruiser. The issue was caused by errant data broadcast through the 'Enform' service, leading to system reboots and customer complaints. The companies halted the problematic data stream, provided instructions for resetting the vehicles’ computers, and offered dealer assistance. The incident highlights the risks associated with increasingly complex car software and the growing use of over-the-air updates to manage vehicle systems.

1622433_1622433.caption: The runway at Maitiga airport in Tripoli was cleared by fire fighters after the air strike
1622433_1622433.article_context: Islamist militants have seized two major oil fields, Bahi and Mabruk, in central Libya after security forces guarding the sites ran out of ammunition and retreated. This development intensifies the ongoing conflict between Libya’s internationally recognized government in Tobruk and the rival Libya Dawn alliance, with both sides carrying out airstrikes against each other. The capture of these oil fields by militants with unclear affiliations further complicates Libya’s instability, as the country continues to struggle with lawlessness and economic decline since the 2011 ousting of Muammar Gaddafi. The United Nations is attempting to mediate peace negotiations between the warring parties.

347872_347872.caption: People celebrate in front of the Greek parliament as the people of Greece reject the debt bailout by creditors on July 6 2015 in Athens Greece
347872_347872.article_context: Global financial markets faced renewed instability after Greek voters overwhelmingly rejected the bailout terms set by international creditors, heightening concerns about Greece potentially leaving the eurozone. Asian stocks fell sharply, with notable declines in Japan and Hong Kong, while U.S. markets were expected to open down. The vote shocked expectations and strengthened Greece's negotiating position, raising uncertainty and fear in markets. Investors moved toward safe-haven assets like U.S. Treasuries, affecting bond yields and currency values, with the euro falling against the dollar. While Greek banks risk running out of cash soon, analysts anticipate resumed negotiations with creditors, hoping for a possible deal to keep Greece in the eurozone, though market volatility is expected to persist for weeks.

1582385_1582385.caption: A car in Newtownabbey was damaged when a tree fell across the Antrim Road close to Belfast Zoo
1582385_1582385.article_context: Northern Ireland Electricity reported that power has been mostly restored after strong winds caused outages affecting nearly 30,000 customers. Major disruptions included the temporary closure of Belfast's Christmas market, blocked roads from fallen trees, and interrupted ferry and rail services. NIE's engineers, with support from teams across Northern Ireland, worked to fix all known faults and aimed to restore service to remaining customers by Friday morning.

293461_293461.caption: Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump disembarks his campaign jet with New Jersey Governor Chris Christie for a rally at Millington Regional Jetport Feb 27 2016 in Millington TN
293461_293461.article_context: A USA TODAY investigation found that Donald Trump's businesses have been involved in over 100 lawsuits and disputes concerning unpaid taxes or contested property assessments since the late 1980s. Trump companies have repeatedly disputed tax bills and delayed payments, prompting state authorities in New York and New Jersey to file liens and take legal action to recover overdue taxes, which were eventually paid after lengthy battles. Trump’s strategy centers on minimizing property values for tax purposes while declaring much higher valuations on financial disclosure forms, allowing him to aggressively reduce his tax bills—sometimes saving millions. This approach is unprecedented among major party presidential nominees and has drawn public scrutiny, especially as Trump continues to refuse to release his personal federal tax returns.

1593642_1593642.caption: The Barclays settlement involves two separate lawsuits brought by the FHFA
1593642_1593642.article_context: Barclays reached a $280 million settlement with the US Federal Housing and Finance Authority to resolve allegations that it misled Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during the housing crisis. The settlement covers two FHFA lawsuits and will not affect Barclays' earnings. This agreement is part of a broader effort by the FHFA, which has filed 18 lawsuits regarding over $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities from the housing bubble, with previous major settlements including $9 billion from Bank of America and $4 billion from JP Morgan Chase.

1654351_1654351.caption: Labour says David Cameron s green days are behind him
1654351_1654351.article_context: At its annual conference, the Labour Party outlined key policies ahead of the upcoming general election, focusing on boosting NHS funding by £2.5bn through new taxes including a mansion tax on properties over £2m, a corporate tax crackdown, and a tobacco levy. Labour pledged faster NHS appointments, a higher minimum wage, and bans on zero-hours contracts, alongside increases to housing, energy, and childcare support. The party aims to cap welfare increases, abolish the 'bedroom tax', freeze energy prices, cap rent and rail fare rises, and build 200,000 new homes annually. Plans include stricter border controls and immigration policies, more support for small businesses, qualified teachers in schools, expanded childcare, and promoting green jobs with climate initiatives. Labour also committed to reducing the national deficit without relying on additional borrowing.

1528443_1528443.caption: Factory workers protested in Noida near the Indian capital Delhi
1528443_1528443.article_context: Millions of workers across India launched a nationwide strike to protest the Modi government’s economic policies, which they argue favor businesses at the expense of job security and public welfare. Major trade unions, representing sectors like banking, manufacturing, and mining, are demanding that the government abandon plans to privatize state-run companies and revise labor laws. The strike caused disruptions in banks, public transport, schools, and businesses, especially in states with strong union presence such as West Bengal and Kerala. The protest reflects growing tensions over government reform efforts, even as India’s economy shows signs of growth.

280671_280671.caption: Federal Reserve Chairman Janet Yellen testifies before a Joint Economic Committee hearing on Capitol Hill December 3 2015 in Washington DC
280671_280671.article_context: Retirees now need to save much more—up to $1 million—to obtain half of their income from safe investments like Treasuries, due to historically low interest rates maintained by the Federal Reserve. Even with an expected small rate hike, the increase will not significantly improve retirement incomes, which have dropped sharply since 1981. The decline in income from low-risk investments, coupled with the disappearance of traditional pension plans, means retirees today must work longer, save more, or take on higher investment risks to sustain their retirement, none of which are ideal options.

82945_82945.caption: Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump is proposing the most generous student loan repayment plan REUTERSEric Thayer
82945_82945.article_context: Donald Trump unveiled a new student loan repayment plan that would cap payments at 12.5 percent of a borrower's income and allow for loan forgiveness after 15 years, which is more generous than existing federal programs. His proposal would consolidate current repayment plans and apply to both federal and private student loans, but lacks specific cost projections and has drawn criticism for its potential fiscal impact. Trump also called for colleges to use their endowments to reduce tuition and student debt, and pledged to cut federal regulations to lower administrative costs. The plan stands in contrast to traditional Republican views on fiscal responsibility and has sparked debate about its effectiveness and the underlying causes of college affordability.

417330_417330.caption: Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton delivers a speech on the US economy at Futuramic Tool Engineering August 11 2016 in Warren Michigan
417330_417330.article_context: Hillary Clinton unveiled an economic plan focused on raising taxes for the wealthy to fund initiatives that support workers and low- and middle-income families, such as free or lower-cost education, paid family leave, childcare tax credits, and a higher minimum wage. Her plan also outlines increased infrastructure spending and targeted tariffs against trade violators, while opposing broad trade agreements like the Trans-Pacific Partnership. Unlike Donald Trump’s proposal to broadly lower corporate and small business taxes, Clinton’s plan centers on new taxes for certain corporations and financial transactions but does not address small business tax relief. The overall approach prioritizes social programs and worker protections over broad regulatory relief for businesses.

1461375_1461375.caption: The US says Bank Rossiya has links to senior Russian officials
1461375_1461375.article_context: Visa and MasterCard blocked credit card services to several Russian banks linked to individuals targeted by US sanctions, affecting Bank Rossiya, SMP Bank, and affiliated institutions. The move prompted criticism from Russian officials, including President Putin who pledged support for the affected banks. Western sanctions and asset freezes over Ukraine led to a sharp drop in Russian stocks, with rating agencies S&P and Fitch downgrading Russia’s economic outlook to 'negative.' Additionally, Germany suspended approval of all defense-related exports to Russia. These measures signal escalating financial and economic pressure on Russia in response to the situation in Ukraine.

1670370_1670370.caption: Jeroen Dijsselbloem says the Eurogroup will listen to the Greek government s ideas
1670370_1670370.article_context: Greece's new anti-austerity government has presented its first alternative debt proposals to eurozone finance ministers in Brussels, seeking to replace 30% of its bailout obligations with a new reform plan and avoid extending the current EU-IMF financial program that ends on February 28. The government wants a 'bridge agreement' to maintain funding while negotiating a longer-term deal, but eurozone leaders insist Greece must honor existing bailout terms. The situation is tense, with large public demonstrations in support of the government's stance and concerns that a failure to reach an agreement could risk Greece's exit from the eurozone and trigger wider financial instability.

254849_254849.caption: Katy Perry performs at rally for Hillary Clinton in Des Moines Iowa Oct 24 2015
254849_254849.article_context: According to Forbes magazine, Katy Perry was the highest-earning female musician between June 2014 and June 2015, bringing in $135 million due to her successful world tour, hit songs, and major endorsement deals, surpassing Taylor Swift, who earned $80 million. Despite their ongoing rivalry, both artists continue to achieve significant financial success. Perry has also been prominent as a celebrity supporter of Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign. Other top female earners on Forbes’ list include Fleetwood Mac, Lady Gaga, and Beyoncé, all boosted by touring and lucrative business ventures. Forbes predicts Swift may be a frontrunner for next year’s top spot, while the male top-earners list is expected soon.

78085_78085.caption: Turing Pharmaceuticals CEO Martin Shkreli this month on CBS
78085_78085.article_context: Democratic lawmakers are demanding answers and congressional hearings from Valeant Pharmaceuticals after the company sharply increased prices for two heart drugs following their acquisition, echoing public outrage over a similar price hike by Turing Pharmaceuticals. Valeant tripled the price of Nitropress and increased Isuprel’s price more than sixfold, prompting lawmakers including Sen. Claire McCaskill, Sen. Bernie Sanders, and Rep. Elijah Cummings to seek explanations. Valeant has refused to provide requested documents, citing confidentiality, and maintains that the price hikes do not affect patient access since the drugs are used in hospital settings. Legislators are pressing for more transparency and accountability regarding these corporate drug pricing practices.

384843_384843.caption: Fifty years after Kennedy s assassination USA NOW host Carly Mallenbaum talks about the different conspiracy theories surrounding the tragedy
384843_384843.article_context: The assassination of President John F. Kennedy on November 22, 1963, caused a significant but brief shock to the U.S. stock market, with the S&P 500 dropping 2.8% and the New York Stock Exchange closing early. Although the event ranked among the biggest market shocks in 70 years, stocks quickly rebounded within two days, reflecting Wall Street’s tendency to recover rapidly after major, but non-economic, crises. The article highlights how markets generally bounce back from sudden shocks, as long as there is confidence in underlying economic stability and orderly political succession.

1469651_1469651.caption: Milan rally Thousands of trade union members protested across Italy
1469651_1469651.article_context: A nationwide general strike has disrupted transportation and closed schools and hospitals across Italy, as thousands of workers protested against government plans to reform labour laws. Trade unions are opposing Prime Minister Matteo Renzi's proposed 'Jobs Act,' fearing it will threaten job security and increase the risk of dismissals, while Renzi argues these reforms are necessary to boost Italy's struggling economy and lower youth unemployment. The strike marks a significant rift between unions and the centre-left government, with some members of Renzi's own party joining the demonstrations, highlighting internal discord amid ongoing economic challenges.

1566449_1566449.caption: Petrobras CEO Graca Foster has been forced to resign over the scandal
1566449_1566449.article_context: The massive corruption scandal at Brazil's state oil company Petrobras has led to the resignation of CEO Maria das Gracas Foster and five senior executives, as the company grapples with allegations of bribery, inflated contracts, and illegal payments to political parties. The ongoing police investigation, known as Operation Car Wash, has intensified with the questioning of the Workers' Party treasurer, escalating the case's political impact. The crisis has severely damaged Petrobras's finances, causing its share value to plummet and delaying the release of audited financial results, while also negatively affecting Brazil’s broader economy. The new leadership faces the challenge of restoring confidence, calculating the scale of losses, and limiting further economic fallout, as the scandal continues to overshadow Brazil's reputation and prospects.

257366_257366.caption: Citing security concerns Apple has filed a motion to vacate an order that would have required the company to help access Syed Farook s iPhone Video provided by Newsy
257366_257366.article_context: A large coalition of tech companies, including industry giants like Google, Facebook, Amazon, Microsoft, and Twitter, have filed legal briefs supporting Apple in its refusal to help the FBI unlock an iPhone used by a San Bernardino mass shooter. The companies argue that compelling Apple to create software to override its security threatens privacy, digital security, and sets a dangerous legal precedent. Law enforcement groups and some victims' families support the FBI’s position, citing public safety concerns. The case has generated widespread debate, dividing public opinion and highlighting tensions between privacy rights and law enforcement needs, with a hearing scheduled for March 22 in federal court.

913099_913099.caption: Playing hard to get Trent Reznor left of Nine Inch Nails had his app rejected by Apple
913099_913099.article_context: Apple's strict App Store approval policies have sparked controversy after rejecting a Nine Inch Nails app for violating content guidelines, despite the absence of parental controls on current iPhone software. Trent Reznor criticized Apple's inconsistency, highlighting that explicit content is still accessible through other means on the device. The upcoming iPhone OS 3.0 update promises parental controls and age-specific app sections, but developers remain frustrated by Apple's opaque and inconsistent approval process, with concerns that these issues may persist and drive developers to other platforms.

1076675_1076675.caption: James Bond 007 Blood Stone watch where you point that gun Danny boy
1076675_1076675.article_context: James Bond: Blood Stone, released alongside the rebooted GoldenEye, was anticipated due to its strong production values, a story by Bond screenwriter Bruce Feirstein, and voice acting from Daniel Craig and Judi Dench. Despite these strengths, the game disappoints with its short playtime, repetitive gameplay, poorly animated cutscenes, and lack of challenge. While driving sequences provide some excitement, most of the game consists of monotonous shootouts and unvaried hand-to-hand takedowns, ultimately making Blood Stone a missed opportunity for the Bond franchise.

447357_447357.caption: High school student Cameron DAmbrosio posted that the White House was a federal house of horrors
447357_447357.article_context: Cameron D'Ambrosio, an 18-year-old Massachusetts high school student, has been jailed without bail for over a month after posting a controversial Facebook message referencing the Boston Marathon bombings and the White House. He faces up to 20 years in prison for 'communicating a terroristic threat,' but has pleaded not guilty. Authorities have delayed proving probable cause, extending his detention, which free speech advocates criticize as prosecutorial overreach and a threat to civil liberties. The case has sparked public campaigns calling for his release and raised concerns over the impact of post-tragedy prosecutions on free expression.

673994_673994.caption: A spectacular car crash Australianstyle from the film Mad Max Is Facebook heading for similar
673994_673994.article_context: The Guardian Technology team highlights key tech stories, including skepticism about Facebook's financial future and its potential impact on ad-supported web businesses, a Microsoft Research team establishing a new data sorting record with fewer resources, and the rise in sophisticated mobile malware disguised as working apps like Angry Birds Space. Other notable points include data suggesting the iPhone’s popularity is partly due to female users, Apple maintaining mobile PC market leadership thanks to iPad sales, claims that Ryanair manipulates prices for returning website visitors, and a European Commission statement warning Google to change its business practices to avoid antitrust penalties.

527853_527853.caption: Andy Burnham We warned David Cameron 18 months ago that greater safeguards were needed on the use of data in the NHS
527853_527853.article_context: Private health firms such as Bupa have been granted government approval to access sensitive and identifiable NHS patient records under a new arrangement, with costs starting at £140 per individual. This data includes intimate medical histories and can identify patients through demographic details. The move, intended to aid life sciences companies, has sparked criticism and privacy concerns from campaigners and opposition politicians, who argue that the NHS is effectively selling patient data without sufficient safeguards or consent from individuals. The Health and Social Care Information Centre states that identifiable data is only provided when legally justified or with patient consent and is typically anonymized, while calls to suspend the practice and investigate have been made by the opposition.

496981_496981.caption: The Apple logo at the Yerba Buena Center for Arts in San Francisco The tech firm is due to release it latest results Wednesday
496981_496981.article_context: Apple is expected to report its first profit decline in nine years, amid falling shares and increased competition from rivals like Samsung and HTC. Despite potentially record iPhone sales last quarter, concerns have arisen about Apple's ability to sustain momentum after new product launches, with sales now dropping more quickly than in previous years. Analysts are divided: some argue Apple's compressed product cycle and fierce market competition threaten its long-term growth, while others believe the company still has room to expand through new products, such as more affordable iPhones, and may continue to redefine the tech industry. Apple's lack of major new releases since Steve Jobs's death has intensified speculation about whether it can deliver another groundbreaking product.

820883_820883.caption: The UK s broadband network will not be fast enough to deal with the internet needs of the future says a House of Lords report
820883_820883.article_context: A House of Lords committee has criticized the UK government's broadband strategy, warning that public funds are being spent on a network that will soon be inadequate and might require costly upgrades or replacement. The report highlights that the current approach, favoring BT for rural broadband expansion, risks stifling competition and widening the digital divide. The committee urges the government to adopt a more ambitious, future-proof vision—such as building a national network of fibre hubs—rather than relying on outdated speed targets and infrastructure. The report calls for long-term solutions to ensure equal broadband access and competition, arguing that broadband should be treated as a key utility across the UK.

1122365_1122365.caption: Scott Thompson will be replaced by Ross Levinsohn with immediate effect
1122365_1122365.article_context: Yahoo CEO Scott Thompson resigned following revelations that he had falsely claimed a computer science degree, a controversy intensified by activist shareholder Daniel Loeb. Thompson’s departure was also influenced by his recent diagnosis of thyroid cancer. Ross Levinsohn was named interim CEO, and Yahoo announced several board changes, including the appointment of Loeb and Fred Amoroso as chairman. These leadership changes come as Yahoo continues to lose market share in online advertising to competitors like Google and Facebook, prompting analysts to view the management overhaul as a necessary reset for the struggling company.

887147_887147.caption: The biggest event in the eightyear history of Google News The US presidential election November 2008
887147_887147.article_context: Google News, launched in the aftermath of September 11, turned eight years old and has become a major global news portal, indexing stories from over 50,000 sources in 30 languages. The platform was founded by Krishna Bharat to address the challenge of accessing information during major events. Over the years, Google News has influenced both how news is consumed online and the publishing industry, facing criticism for not sufficiently compensating news publishers. Its biggest stories have included the election of Barack Obama in 2008, the Iraq war in 2003, Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and other major world events.

551011_551011.caption: David Cameron and Home secretary Theresa May are pushing ahead with the Investigatory Powers Act despite doubts that it will be effective in combating terrorism
551011_551011.article_context: David Cameron's government introduced the Snooper’s Charter, mandating technology companies like Facebook and Google to provide decrypted user messages to law enforcement, effectively banning strong cryptography. Experts argue that this measure will not increase security or stop serious criminals, as determined individuals can easily access secure, independent encryption tools. To effectively enforce the policy, the government would need to implement increasingly draconian controls over software and hardware, including restricting non-approved programs, blocking global internet resources, and even redesigning computers to run only sanctioned applications. Critics warn such measures are both impractical and dangerously authoritarian, fundamentally threatening privacy and civil liberties without achieving the intended security goals.

722172_722172.caption: When GamerGate meets One Direction it will break the internet read on for more predictions for Twitter s future
722172_722172.article_context: The article reflects on Twitter’s decade of influence since Jack Dorsey's first tweet in 2006, highlighting its evolution through trending topics, political movements, and viral moments. Looking ahead, it humorously predicts future changes for Twitter, such as the removal of character limits, new reaction buttons, timeline experiments, and increased AI involvement. The article also satirizes the platform’s challenges, including celebrity controversies, expert predictions of Twitter’s demise, and persistent issues with online harassment.

1063672_1063672.caption: Samsung has been locked in a patent battle with Apple over the flagship device since April
1063672_1063672.article_context: A German court has upheld a nationwide ban on the sale of Samsung's Galaxy Tab, ruling that its design closely resembles Apple's iPad following Apple’s second legal claim. The decision is part of Apple's ongoing international patent battle against Samsung, aiming to block the sale of Galaxy tablets and smartphones in multiple countries. Samsung, which has also counter-sued Apple over wireless patents, said it would appeal the ruling, arguing it harms consumer choice and restricts innovation. The ban prevents further distribution to German retailers, though they may sell existing inventory.

1027048_1027048.caption: Mark Zuckerberg has ruled out the idea of a dislike button on Facebook
1027048_1027048.article_context: During a public Q&A session, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced that the company is exploring ways for users to express a wider range of emotions beyond the 'like' button, acknowledging that 'liking' posts about misfortune can feel inappropriate. While Facebook will not introduce a 'dislike' button, Zuckerberg emphasized the importance of finding a positive way for users to share their feelings. No immediate changes are planned, but the goal is to enhance user expression and keep the platform constructive.

971564_971564.caption: Swedish court dismisses action from rightsholders against Sweden s secondlargest internet service provider over access to the Pirate Bay
971564_971564.article_context: A Swedish court has ruled that internet service providers in Sweden, including Bredbandsbolaget, cannot be forced to block access to the file-sharing site The Pirate Bay or be held responsible for their users’ copyright infringements. The lawsuit from major film and music companies was rejected, and the rightsholders were ordered to pay legal costs. While the decision marks a setback for the copyright groups, they may still appeal, leaving open the possibility of future legal action. The Pirate Bay, founded in 2003, remains a prominent target for copyright enforcement efforts in Europe.

859839_859839.caption: Sony Pictures fights back to attempt to stop people downloading its stolen data which included Brad Pitt s new film Fury
859839_859839.article_context: Sony Pictures is reportedly using hacking techniques, specifically distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, to prevent the spread of its stolen data on file-sharing websites. The company is allegedly utilizing Amazon Web Services (AWS) to flood these sites, despite AWS policies that prohibit such activities. The leaked information includes unreleased films, executive pay details, social media credentials, and email archives, causing significant disruption and controversy in Hollywood. The cyberattack on Sony has been speculatively linked to North Korea due to the film The Interview, though the FBI has found no evidence of this connection.

1205661_1205661.caption: Apple has seen declining sales of its iPad line despite of the launch of a thinnner iPad Air 2 and iPad Mini 3
1205661_1205661.article_context: Apple's planned 12.9-inch 'iPad Pro,' which targets business users with features like potential USB ports and keyboard/mouse support, has been delayed due to production issues and is now expected to begin production in the second half of the year. The delay comes as Apple faces declining iPad sales and increased competition from large-screen smartphones. The new, larger iPad—possibly launching in October—aims to revive sales by appealing to business customers, bolstered by Apple's partnership with IBM to offer specialized business applications.

880583_880583.caption: Staff at Spotify s offices in Stockholm The new parental leave policy comes despite continuing losses
880583_880583.article_context: Spotify announced a global policy granting employees up to six months of fully paid parental leave, backdated to cover children born after January 1, 2013. The initiative aims to foster a healthy work-family balance, offering flexible return-to-work options for all 1,600 staff worldwide. This policy is significantly more generous than legal requirements in countries like the UK and the US. Despite ongoing financial losses, Spotify says its Swedish-inspired culture supports such progressive benefits, underlining its commitment to gender equality and employee well-being.

1230606_1230606.caption: dianainheaven I follow Twitter news feeds which often announce celebrity deaths before Sky and the BBC so it looks as if Diana is getting the scoop
1230606_1230606.article_context: The article profiles several popular parody Twitter accounts in the UK, highlighting the creators behind each one and their motivations. These accounts include @CherylKerl, a comedic Geordie version of Cheryl Cole; @chilean_miner, which imagined the lives of trapped Chilean miners with light-hearted tweets; @CatBinLady, a satirical character inspired by a viral news story; @DrSamuelJohnson, a playful take on the 18th-century lexicographer; and @dianainheaven, which humorously depicts Princess Diana tweeting from the afterlife. Each account rapidly gained thousands of followers and media attention, showing how humour and clever character creation can drive success on social media.

1239460_1239460.caption: It was reported in November that conditions at an Amazon warehouse could cause mental and physical illness according to one of Britain s leading experts on stress at work
1239460_1239460.article_context: A Change.org petition calling on Amazon UK chief Jeff Bezos to pay agency staff the living wage has garnered over 40,000 signatures in two days. The campaign, launched by activist Emily Kenway, highlights concerns that the 15,000 temporary workers hired for the holiday period are paid insufficient wages and subjected to harsh workplace policies, including strict sick leave and break rules, long shifts, and intensive performance monitoring. Despite repeated criticism over working conditions in its warehouses, Amazon maintains that its pay and benefits meet industry standards. The issue has sparked wider debate about the treatment of low-paid workers and the ethics of large corporations.

822709_822709.caption: Mexico s Francisco Palencia Guillermo Franco and Andres Guardado celebrate a goal ESPN will televise Mexico s World Cup match against South Africa in 3D
822709_822709.article_context: On June 11, 2010, ESPN launched the first dedicated 3D television network during the World Cup, marking a significant shift in home TV consumption. The move is seen as the next major step after HDTV and Blu-ray, though widespread adoption faces hurdles including high costs and the need for special 3D glasses. Inspired by the success of the 3D film Avatar, other broadcasters like Discovery, in partnership with Imax and Sony, are planning 3D channels, while major tech companies are racing to produce compatible televisions. Industry experts believe that, despite challenges, growing demand will drive further advancements in 3D home entertainment.

455101_455101.caption: Samsung is deliberately disabling Microsoft s crucial Windows Update on some laptops leaving users vulnerable to hacking
455101_455101.article_context: Samsung has been found to disable Windows Update on some of its computers via its SW Update tool, potentially leaving users without critical security patches and vulnerable to cyber threats. Independent Microsoft engineer Patrick Barker raised concerns that Samsung’s software would turn off Windows Update even if users re-enabled it, citing driver compatibility as the company’s reason. Security experts criticized the move, warning it resembled tactics used by malware. Samsung denies blocking Windows updates entirely and claims users can choose when to update, but the issue has raised significant concerns about user safety and device security.

680146_680146.caption: Gen David Petraeus has previously said US online psychological operations are aimed at countering extremist ideology and propaganda
680146_680146.article_context: The US military has awarded a contract to a Californian company to develop software enabling personnel to manage multiple fake online identities and influence social media discussions with pro-American propaganda. This 'online persona management service,' linked to Operation Earnest Voice, aims to counter extremist ideology and propaganda on non-English foreign language sites in the Middle East and Central Asia. The project, not targeting US audiences and major platforms like Facebook or Twitter, has raised concerns about potential misuse, legal issues, and broader implications for internet free speech and manipulation.

479358_479358.caption: CIA director John Brennan on the top challenges facing US and global security and addressed questions related to Friday s terror attack in Paris
479358_479358.article_context: In the wake of the Paris attacks by Islamic State militants, US and European officials reignited debate over whether governments should have 'back-door' access to encrypted communications, claiming such security measures may hinder efforts to track terrorists. Despite little evidence that attackers used encryption, intelligence and law enforcement leaders called the incident a 'wakeup call' and pressured for reviews and possible extension of surveillance powers. Privacy advocates and tech experts opposed these demands, arguing that back doors would increase vulnerability to hackers and criminals, and that there is no technically feasible way to provide access only to the 'good guys.' Conflicting reports about platforms like PlayStation and secure messaging apps have fueled the debate, which threatens the fragile cooperation between Silicon Valley and government just as recent cybersecurity legislation encourages information sharing.

660290_660290.caption: 55 Savushkina Street St Petersburg said to be the headquarters of Russia s troll army
660290_660290.article_context: The Obama administration revealed that the US federal government suffered a major cyberattack, compromising the data of up to four million current and former employees. While initial suspicions pointed toward China, they denied any involvement, and the hackers’ motives remain unclear. The article also discusses the rise of 'troll factories,' particularly in Russia, which employ paid bloggers to spread propaganda and manipulate online opinion, contributing to distrust and misinformation. These digital tactics are part of a broader trend of information warfare, increasingly used by both state and non-state actors to subvert and polarize societies. The piece calls for a commitment to honesty in digital engagement, highlighting the dangers of misinformation and propaganda on global stability.

792424_792424.caption: Spanish lawyer Mario Costeja fought successfully for a ruling by the European Court of Justice which grants individuals in the EU the right to be forgotten online
792424_792424.article_context: The European Court of Justice recently ruled in favor of the 'right to be forgotten,' highlighting the growing tension between privacy and freedom of speech in the digital age. This decision marks an important step in recognizing complex issues about personal data and online identity, demanding innovative legal and technological solutions beyond outdated frameworks. The article argues for nuanced debate and warns against oversimplifying the conflict between privacy and free speech, while also cautioning against fragmented or monopolized control over information. Ultimately, it calls for ethical consideration and collaborative efforts to balance fundamental rights in our increasingly 'onlife' society, as illustrated by Google’s acceptance of requests from Europeans to remove search links.

1270243_1270243.caption: A group of performers unfurl the Microsoft logo as part of the Windows Vista launch in January 2007 The operating system came with bugs galore
1270243_1270243.article_context: Windows 10 represents a critical release for Microsoft, aiming to unify the user experience across devices—from desktops to tablets and smartphones—through a common platform and universal apps. To succeed, it must overcome the negative perceptions left by Windows Vista and Windows 8, offer a familiar yet modern interface, and ensure a seamless upgrade process, especially for existing Windows 7 users. Microsoft’s broader challenge lies in convincing users to leave older versions and persuading manufacturers and developers to support its new vision, particularly in the smartphone market. The success of Windows 10 is pivotal for Microsoft’s continued relevance in computing.

921647_921647.caption: Share issue Mark Zuckerberg rings the Nasdaq opening bell as Facebook goes public
921647_921647.article_context: Facebook's highly anticipated May 2012 initial public offering (IPO), valued at $100bn, marked a pivotal moment for the company, instantly making many employees and investors enormously wealthy. However, widespread speculation, technical glitches, and concerns over the company's advertising model and lack of transparency quickly led to a sharp decline in Facebook's share price, which lost nearly half its value within months. Lawsuits from small investors followed, accusing Facebook and its underwriters of withholding crucial information about downgrades in revenue forecasts. CEO Mark Zuckerberg faced criticism for prioritizing the company's mission of openness over profit-driven strategies, and struggled with investor confidence and the challenges of monetizing mobile users. Despite reaching one billion users, Facebook's stock failed to recover, leaving its long-term status as a 'utility' and its valuation uncertain.

755466_755466.caption: Google has bought UK startup Plink for an undisclosed sum
755466_755466.article_context: Google has made its first UK acquisition by purchasing mobile visual search startup Plink, which was founded by Oxford PhD students Mark Cummins and James Philbin. Plink developed PlinkArt, a popular app that identifies artworks from user photos, attracting over 50,000 downloads soon after launch. The deal will see the founders join Google to work on its visual search project, Google Goggles, in California. The acquisition, prompted by Plink's success in the Android Developer Challenge, is part of Google's strategy to expand by acquiring innovative startups.

469409_469409.caption: Google pulled out of China amid a row over government censorship and hacking of its systems including Gmail accounts used by activists
469409_469409.article_context: Classified US diplomatic cables reveal that a senior member of China's Communist politburo orchestrated the hacking attack on Google, after finding personal criticism in search results. The cyber assault targeted Google's operations in mainland China and the Gmail accounts of dissidents, prompting Google to withdraw from the Chinese market in January, relocating its operations to Hong Kong. The leaked cables indicate the attack was politically motivated and involved collaboration among top Chinese officials, but there is no confirmation that the highest leaders, such as President Hu Jintao, were aware. The incident heightened tensions over internet censorship and drew public support for Google from US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

1086817_1086817.caption: Amazon quietly abandoned its practice of pooling European sales in Luxembourg last month and opened taxable branches in its main European markets including the UK
1086817_1086817.article_context: Amazon generated £5.3bn in UK sales in 2014 but paid only £11.9m in UK tax, as most sales were channeled through its Luxembourg subsidiary, avoiding higher UK taxation. This practice is part of a broader trend among tech companies of diverting profits to low-tax jurisdictions, which has prompted international tax reform efforts led by the G20 and OECD. In response, the UK introduced a 25% tax rate targeting such arrangements, and Amazon has recently begun processing sales through taxable UK branches.
